name: Puri Bhaji
cuisine: Maharashtrian / Mumbai (batata bhaji with puri; Udupi-restaurant and home breakfast across Mumbai, also a railway-platform snack in central India)

ingredients.name: Water (for the dough)
ingredients.householdMeasure: 2 tbsp + 1 tsp, added a little at a time

ingredients.name: Sunflower or groundnut oil (for deep-frying)
ingredients.householdMeasure: about 1 cup in a small kadai

ingredients.name: Ginger (adrak)
ingredients.householdMeasure: ½-inch piece, finely chopped or grated

ingredients.name: Onion (pyaz/kanda)
ingredients.householdMeasure: ½ small onion, thinly sliced or chopped

equipment: Pressure cooker (1.5–3 litre) for the potatoes
Mixing bowl (paraat or any wide bowl) for the dough
Small pan or kadai (about 18 cm) for the bhaji, with a lid (a steel plate works as a lid)
Separate small deep kadai for frying (deep enough for about 4 cm of oil)
Slotted spoon (jhara) for pressing and lifting the puris
Plate lined with a wire rack or paper towel for draining
Measuring spoons and cup (a normal teaspoon and a steel glass are fine stand-ins)
Optional: a kitchen thermometer (oil at about 180–190 °C)

steps.title: Wash the potatoes
steps.text: Rinse 150 g potato (1 large or 2 small) under running water, rubbing off any soil.
steps.visualCue: Clean skin, no mud
steps.videoShot: Potatoes rubbed under a running tap.

steps.title: Pressure-cook the potatoes
steps.text: Put them whole, unpeeled, in the cooker with 1 cup water, close and cook on medium for 3 whistles.
steps.tip: Cut a very large potato in half so it cooks through.
steps.visualCue: Third whistle
steps.cameraCheck: The closed cooker on the flame

steps.title: Turn off and let the pressure drop
steps.text: Switch off the heat and leave the cooker closed while you make the dough.
steps.visualCue: The float valve drops; no hiss when the weight is nudged

steps.title: Measure the flour and salt
steps.text: Put 60 g whole wheat flour (½ cup) and a pinch (0.5 g) salt in a bowl and mix.
steps.visualCue: Flour heap with salt mixed in

steps.title: Rub in the oil
steps.text: Add ½ tsp (3 g) oil and rub it into the flour with your fingertips.
steps.visualCue: Flour looks slightly crumbly and holds a shape when pressed
steps.cameraCheck: A pinch of flour pressed between fingers

steps.title: Add water and knead a stiff dough
steps.text: Add about 32 ml water a little at a time, bringing the flour together, then knead.
steps.tip: Stiff dough is the secret of puris that puff and stay less oily; soft roti-style dough drinks oil. If too stiff to knead, wet your hand rather than adding more water.
steps.visualCue: A smooth, firm, non-sticky dough, stiffer than roti dough; a finger press leaves a dent that does not spring back fully
steps.videoShot: Knuckles pressing and folding the dough.

steps.title: Rest the dough
steps.text: Cover the bowl with a lid or damp cloth.
steps.visualCue: Dough feels slightly smoother and relaxed
steps.videoShot: A lid placed over the dough bowl.

steps.title: Peel the potatoes
steps.text: Open the cooker, drain, and peel the warm potatoes.
steps.tip: Cool them under the tap for 30 seconds if too hot to hold.
steps.visualCue: Skin slips off easily; flesh is soft right through
steps.videoShot: Skin peeling off a boiled potato.

steps.title: Break up the potatoes
steps.text: Chop or crumble into rough 1.5 cm pieces, leaving some smaller crumbs.
steps.visualCue: Mix of chunks and crumbs, not mashed
steps.videoShot: A knife breaking potatoes into chunks.

steps.title: Slice the onion
steps.text: Thinly slice or finely chop ½ small onion (40 g).
steps.visualCue: Thin, even slices, about ⅓ cup

steps.title: Chop the chilli and ginger
steps.text: Finely chop 1 green chilli (4 g) and ½-inch ginger (3 g).
steps.visualCue: Small, even bits
steps.cameraCheck: Chilli and ginger on the board

steps.title: Chop the coriander
steps.text: Chop 2 tsp (3 g) coriander leaves.
steps.visualCue: Fresh green, not bruised

steps.title: Heat the oil for the bhaji
steps.text: Put the small pan on medium heat with 1½ tsp (7 g) oil.
steps.visualCue: Oil shimmers

steps.title: Crackle the mustard seeds
steps.text: Add ¼ tsp (1 g) mustard seeds.
steps.tip: Keep the lid handy; the seeds jump.
steps.visualCue: Seeds pop and jump; crackling sound

steps.title: Fry the cumin and urad dal
steps.text: Add ⅛ tsp (0.5 g) cumin and ½ tsp (2 g) urad dal; stir.
steps.tip: Lower the heat if it browns too fast; burnt dal tastes bitter.
steps.visualCue: Urad dal turns light golden; nutty smell
steps.cameraCheck: The golden dal in the oil

steps.title: Add curry leaves, chilli, ginger and hing
steps.text: Add 6–8 curry leaves, the chilli, the ginger and a small pinch of hing.
steps.visualCue: Leaves crackle and turn glossy and crisp at the edges

steps.title: Cook the onion
steps.text: Add the onion and stir on medium.
steps.visualCue: Soft and translucent, just turning pale gold at the edges

steps.title: Add the turmeric
steps.text: Lower the heat and stir in ⅛ tsp (0.4 g) turmeric.
steps.visualCue: Onion turns yellow; no raw smell after a few seconds

steps.title: Add the potatoes and salt
steps.text: Add the potatoes and 2 g (⅓ tsp) salt; toss gently.
steps.visualCue: Every piece evenly yellow

steps.title: Simmer with water
steps.text: Sprinkle 60 ml (¼ cup) water, cover and simmer on low, then lightly press a few pieces with the spatula.
steps.visualCue: Moist, lightly bound, soft bhaji with no pool of water (dry, not gravy)
steps.cameraCheck: The bhaji with the lid lifted
steps.videoShot: Spatula pressing a few potato pieces.

steps.title: Finish the bhaji
steps.text: Turn off the heat, squeeze in 1 tsp (5 ml) lemon juice, add the coriander, stir and cover to keep warm.
steps.visualCue: Bright yellow bhaji with green flecks; fresh lemony smell

steps.title: Divide the dough
steps.text: Knead the rested dough for 20 seconds and divide into 4 equal balls (about 24 g each).
steps.visualCue: 4 smooth, crack-free balls, each a little smaller than a lemon

steps.title: Roll the puris
steps.text: Smear a drop of oil on the board, and roll each ball into a 10 cm circle, about 2 mm thick, keeping rolled puris under a cloth.
steps.tip: Use oil, not dry flour, for rolling; dry flour burns in the frying oil and darkens it.
steps.visualCue: Even thickness, no thin spots or tears, edges not thicker than the centre
steps.cameraCheck: One rolled puri on the board
steps.videoShot: Rolling pin moving over a puri.

steps.title: Heat the frying oil
steps.text: Heat about 250 ml oil in the deep kadai on medium-high.
steps.tip: If the test piece sinks and stays down, the oil is too cold and puris will be oily; if it browns at once, it is too hot.
steps.visualCue: A pea-size bit of dough dropped in sizzles and rises to the top in 1–2 seconds (about 180–190 °C)
steps.videoShot: A dough piece rising in hot oil.

steps.title: Slide in the first puri
steps.text: Gently slide one puri into the oil from the side, away from you.
steps.tip: Never drop it from a height; hot oil splashes.
steps.visualCue: It sinks briefly and rises

steps.title: Press until it puffs
steps.text: Press gently on the puri with the back of the slotted spoon.
steps.visualCue: It balloons up fully

steps.title: Flip and fry the other side
steps.text: Flip it once and fry.
steps.visualCue: Light golden on both sides, still puffed

steps.title: Drain the puri
steps.text: Lift it out with the slotted spoon, let excess oil drip back for 3–4 seconds and place on the rack or paper.
steps.visualCue: Golden, crisp-edged, puffed

steps.title: Fry the remaining puris
steps.text: Repeat steps 25–28 for the other 3 puris, checking the oil heat between each.
steps.visualCue: 4 evenly golden puris

steps.title: Turn off the heat and serve
steps.text: Turn off the frying oil and serve the 4 hot puris with the bhaji in a bowl.
steps.tip: Let the frying oil cool completely before straining and storing it.
steps.visualCue: Puffed golden puris beside bright yellow bhaji
steps.videoShot: A puri torn and dipped into the bhaji.

reasons: whole-wheat puris and potato give 11 g fibre, decent potassium, B6, niacin and magnesium, no cholesterol and no added sugar, and the bhaji itself is light (7 g oil). But the plate is about 585 kcal and 26 g fat for one breakfast, mostly from deep-frying; it is high in refined starch from potato, only moderate in protein (about 11.5 g) and carries about 1,000 mg sodium. Restaurant puris are often larger and fried in reused oil (more fat, possible trans fats), and the plate often has 5 puris (est.).

researchRating.basis: puri bhaji is a much-loved Mumbai and Maharashtrian breakfast with its own Wikipedia article (traditional breakfast, also sold on railway platforms); century-old Mumbai eateries are known for it (Fodor's calls puri bhaji the trademark dish of Pancham Puriwala near CST, a Tripadvisor review is titled "best place to have puri bhaji in south mumbai", LBB and Curly Tales feature Pancham, and Finely Chopped writes about the puri bhaji at Prakash, Dadar); every major Indian recipe site publishes it (Tarla Dalal, Veg Recipes of India, Spice Up The Curry, Archana's Kitchen, Sanjeev Kapoor's SK Khazana). Points off because it is widely called heavy or unhealthy (Tarla Dalal rates it unhealthy for the deep-frying and potato), and per-recipe review counts were not visible this run. Swiggy dish ratings seen (for example 4.5 from 40 ratings) are not used. Search-result snippets were the only access to these sites this run.

storage: Bhaji: fridge-safe in a closed box for up to 2 days (cool within 1 hour); not good frozen (potato turns grainy). Reheat in a pan with 1–2 tbsp water on low, or microwave covered for 1 minute. Puris: best eaten fresh; they keep 1 day at room temperature in an airtight box (they turn soft and chewy), or 2 days in the fridge; re-crisp on a dry tawa for 30 seconds a side, or in an air fryer or oven at 180 °C for 2–3 min. Do not refry.
leftoverRemix: Batata bhaji toastie or dosa filling. The Maharashtrian bhaji is almost the same as masala-dosa potato filling: spread it inside a dosa or uttapam, or between two slices of bread with green chutney and toast in a sandwich maker. Leftover puris can be crushed into a quick chaat with chopped onion, tomato, green and tamarind chutney and sev.
burnOff: about 8.4 km of running (585 ÷ 70 kcal/km, for a 70 kg adult), or about 11.7 km of brisk walking (about 2 h 20 min at 5 km/h, using about 50 kcal/km for walking) (est.).

navratri.reason: wheat atta, urad dal, onion, turmeric, hing and table salt are avoided in the common vrat rule set; use rajgira or kuttu puris and a cumin-only potato bhaji with sendha namak (Gluten-free / vrat variant; Banana Leaf, Mumbai serves rajgira puri bhaji on its Navratri 2026 menu).

ekadashi.reason: wheat (a grain) and urad dal (a pulse) are avoided on Ekadashi in the most common rule set, along with onion; the same rajgira puri and cumin-potato bhaji with sendha namak fits.

jain.reason: potato, onion and fresh ginger are root vegetables and must all be replaced (dry ginger powder (sonth) is allowed); a Jain version was not researched this run.

ramadan.reason: vegetarian, so no halal-meat issue; better for iftar than sehri, as deep-fried puris are heavy and the plate has about 1,000 mg sodium, which adds to thirst during the fast.

jain.reason: potato, onion and fresh ginger are root vegetables; all three must be swapped (dry ginger powder (sonth) for fresh ginger; potato and onion replaced) and the hing must be checked; see Jain line in Diet variants (not researched yet).

vegan.reason: puris are fried in vegetable oil and the bhaji has no ghee, butter, curd or honey (some homes fry puris in ghee; then it is not vegan).

pescatarian.reason: vegetarian, no meat, so it fits a pescatarian diet.

sattvik.reason: skip the onion (the recipe has no garlic); see Sattvik variant.

glutenFree.reason: the puris are whole-wheat (atta) and most hing sold in India is compounded with wheat flour; swap to rajgira (amaranth) puris and gluten-free hing or no hing (see Gluten-free variant).

dairyFree.reason: no milk, curd, ghee or butter in the main recipe.
